content.title: Will the person you hate most take all your good deeds on Judgment Day?
content.subtitle: How modern backbiting leaves you spiritually bankrupt in the digital age.
content.body:
It is a quarter to eleven at night. Tanvir is lying in bed, scrolling through his phone when a Messenger notification arrives. It is from his close colleague, Rafsan.

“Hey, are you free? I’m sending you a screenshot. Don’t show it to anyone!”

Tanvir opens the image and finds private chats and a voice note from Sajid, a colleague they both know. His sleep disappears instantly. Rafsan quickly types: “See? He acts like a saint at the office! This is his real face.”

Tanvir cannot resist replying: “Come on! I always suspected him!”

What follows is a discussion about Sajid that continues until midnight. They dissect his family problems, personal failures, and minor mistakes, magnifying every detail. After the conversation, Tanvir puts his phone aside and falls asleep feeling strangely satisfied. Not once does he realise what has actually happened in that hour of entertainment.

Why Do We Enjoy Someone Else’s Downfall?

Psychology suggests that discussing someone else's private flaws can create a temporary, false sense of superiority. Rafsan and Tanvir's subconscious minds begin to think: “Sajid is such a terrible person. At least we are much better than him!”

But the reality is that Rafsan exposed Sajid's private conversations to Tanvir today. Tomorrow, he might just as easily expose one of Tanvir's weaknesses to someone else.

Will Your Good Deeds Go to Someone You Cannot Stand?

Throughout the day, Tanvir may not have told a single lie. He may have offered his prayers on time despite his busy schedule and quietly made a small donation. These were the valuable savings he had accumulated throughout the day.

Yet, through just twenty minutes of laughter that night, into whose hands did he hand over those priceless assets? The very person he cannot stand, whose name alone ruins his mood!

The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) once asked the Companions: “Do you know who the truly bankrupt person is?”

They replied: “The person who has no money or possessions.”

He said: “The truly bankrupt person among my Ummah is the one who will come on the Day of Resurrection with prayers, fasting, and zakah. But he insulted someone, slandered another, and violated someone's honour. So, his good deeds will be given to those he wronged as compensation. When his good deeds are exhausted, their sins will be placed upon him, and he will be thrown into Hellfire.”

(Jami' at-Tirmidhi: Hadith 2418)

Think about it. On the scorching plains of the Day of Judgment, when even one's own parents will turn away, what if the rewards of one's Tahajjud, secret charity, dhikr, and Quran recitation begin transferring to someone else's record? Can such a loss ever be compensated?

How to Restrain Yourself

  • Turn Away and Keep Your Distance: Allah Almighty says: “When you see those who engage in mockery or idle talk concerning Our verses, turn away from them until they engage in another conversation.” (Surah Al-An'am: 68). Whenever discussions about someone's faults begin in a gathering or inbox, avoid unnecessary arguments. Leave the chat or gathering until the conversation changes.

  • Protect the Honour of an Absent Brother: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Whoever protects the honour of his brother in his absence, Allah will protect his face from the Fire of Hell on the Day of Judgment.” (Jami' at-Tirmidhi: 1931). When someone sends you a screenshot or exposes another person's private weaknesses, do not encourage it. Simply say, “Neither you nor I are free from mistakes.”

  • Seek Forgiveness When You Make a Mistake: If you unintentionally backbite someone, repent immediately and pray for the forgiveness of the person you spoke about using this supplication: "O Allah, forgive us and forgive him."  (Shu'ab al-Iman: 6786)
